---
title: "04 · Simple Linear Regression: Soil Temperature and Ground Cover"
author: "Maria Jose Ospina"
output: github_document
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 150, fig.path = "figures/"
)
```

Does more vegetation cover keep the soil cooler, and by how much? This report measures the relationship between **ground cover** and **soil temperature**, fits a simple linear regression, checks its assumptions and uses it to make predictions with uncertainty.

```{r libraries}
library(tidyverse)
library(ggpubr)   # scatter plot with correlation
library(knitr)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## 1. Data

Ten plots, each with its percentage of ground cover and its soil temperature.

```{r load}
soil <- read_delim("data/soil_temperature.csv", delim = ";", trim_ws = TRUE) |>
  rename(cover = Cobertura, temperature = Temperatura)

kable(soil, col.names = c("Ground cover (%)", "Soil temperature (°C)"))
```

## 2. Correlation

```{r correlation}
r <- cor(soil$cover, soil$temperature)
cor_test <- cor.test(soil$cover, soil$temperature)
cor_test
```

The Pearson correlation is **r = `r round(r, 2)`**: a strong negative relationship. Plots with more cover have cooler soil.

```{r scatter}
ggscatter(soil, x = "cover", y = "temperature",
          add = "reg.line", conf.int = TRUE,
          color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5,
          add.params = list(color = "#D55E00", fill = "grey85")) +
  stat_cor(method = "pearson", label.x = 75, label.y = 33, r.accuracy = 0.01, p.accuracy = 0.001) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  labs(title = "Soil temperature vs. ground cover",
       x = "Ground cover (%)", y = "Soil temperature (°C)")
```

## 3. The model

$$\text{temperature} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{cover} + \varepsilon$$

```{r model}
model <- lm(temperature ~ cover, data = soil)
summary(model)
anova(model)
```

```{r coefficients}
b0 <- coef(model)[["(Intercept)"]]
b1 <- coef(model)[["cover"]]
r2 <- summary(model)$r.squared
p_value <- summary(model)$coefficients["cover", "Pr(>|t|)"]
ci_b1 <- confint(model)["cover", ]
```

| Term | Estimate | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Intercept (β₀) | `r round(b0, 2)` °C | Expected temperature at 0% cover. It is outside the observed range (56–92%), so it should not be interpreted literally. |
| Slope (β₁) | `r round(b1, 3)` °C per % | Each additional percentage point of cover lowers the soil temperature by about `r round(abs(b1), 2)` °C. |
| R² | `r round(r2, 3)` | Ground cover explains `r round(r2 * 100)`% of the variation in soil temperature. |

The slope is significant (p `r ifelse(p_value < 0.001, "< 0.001", paste("=", round(p_value, 3)))`), and its 95% confidence interval goes from `r round(ci_b1[1], 2)` to `r round(ci_b1[2], 2)` °C per percentage point: it does not include zero.

So **10 more percentage points of cover mean about `r round(abs(b1) * 10, 1)` °C cooler soil**.

## 4. Checking the assumptions

A linear model is only reliable if its residuals (observed − fitted) behave well: no pattern against the fitted values, roughly normal, and with constant spread.

```{r residuals-table}
soil_fit <- soil |>
  mutate(fitted = fitted(model), residual = residuals(model))

kable(soil_fit, digits = 2,
      col.names = c("Cover (%)", "Temperature (°C)", "Fitted (°C)", "Residual (°C)"))
```

```{r residual-plots, fig.height = 3.8, fig.width = 9}
p1 <- ggplot(soil_fit, aes(fitted, residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#0072B2") +
  labs(title = "Residuals vs. fitted", x = "Fitted temperature (°C)", y = "Residual (°C)")

p2 <- ggplot(soil_fit, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq(size = 2.5, color = "#0072B2") +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#D55E00") +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q plot", x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Residual (°C)")

ggarrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

```{r shapiro}
shapiro <- shapiro.test(residuals(model))
shapiro
```

The residuals show no clear pattern and the Shapiro-Wilk test does not reject normality (p = `r round(shapiro$p.value, 2)`). With only `r nrow(soil)` plots, these checks have little power, so the conclusions should be confirmed with more data.

## 5. Predictions with uncertainty

Two kinds of intervals:

- **Confidence interval:** where the **average** temperature of plots with that cover is expected to be.
- **Prediction interval:** where the temperature of **one new plot** is expected to be. It is always wider.

```{r intervals}
grid <- tibble(cover = seq(min(soil$cover), max(soil$cover), length.out = 100))

bands <- grid |>
  bind_cols(
    as_tibble(predict(model, grid, interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)) |>
      rename(fit = fit, conf_low = lwr, conf_high = upr),
    as_tibble(predict(model, grid, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)) |>
      select(pred_low = lwr, pred_high = upr)
  )

ggplot(bands, aes(cover)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = pred_low, ymax = pred_high), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = conf_low, ymax = conf_high), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_segment(data = soil_fit, aes(x = cover, xend = cover, y = temperature, yend = fitted),
               color = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = soil_fit, aes(y = temperature), size = 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Fitted line with 95% confidence and prediction bands",
       subtitle = "Dark band: confidence (mean) · Light band: prediction (single plot) · Red: residuals",
       x = "Ground cover (%)", y = "Soil temperature (°C)")
```

### Prediction at 80% cover

```{r predict-80}
new_plot <- tibble(cover = 80)

pred_80 <- predict(model, new_plot, interval = "prediction", level = 0.95)
conf_80 <- predict(model, new_plot, interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)

tibble(
  interval = c("Confidence (mean of plots)", "Prediction (one plot)"),
  estimate = c(conf_80[, "fit"], pred_80[, "fit"]),
  lower    = c(conf_80[, "lwr"], pred_80[, "lwr"]),
  upper    = c(conf_80[, "upr"], pred_80[, "upr"])
) |> kable(digits = 2)
```

A plot with **80% ground cover** is expected to have a soil temperature of about **`r round(pred_80[, "fit"], 1)` °C**. A single new plot could reasonably fall between `r round(pred_80[, "lwr"], 1)` and `r round(pred_80[, "upr"], 1)` °C.

## Key takeaways

- Ground cover and soil temperature are strongly and negatively related (r = `r round(r, 2)`, R² = `r round(r2, 2)`).
- Each extra percentage point of cover lowers soil temperature by about `r round(abs(b1), 2)` °C within the observed range (56–92%).
- Predictions should always come with an interval, and the model should not be used outside the range of the data.
- With only `r nrow(soil)` plots, the results are a good first estimate but need more data to be confirmed.
